elements.element: Customer owns every deliverable created for Customer.
elements.evidence: The clause instead provides that Type II Materials may be created during performance and that IBM or third parties have all right, title, and interest in them.

elements.element: Customer owns work product created for Customer that is not itself a deliverable.
elements.evidence: There is no Customer ownership provision for work product; service-created Type II Materials remain owned by IBM or third parties.

elements.element: Vendor assigns to Customer all right, title, and interest in deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: No assignment from IBM to Customer appears in the rendered clause.

elements.element: Vendor retains all rights in its pre-existing IP.
elements.evidence: Type II Materials expressly include materials that preexist the Service and in which IBM has all right, title, and interest.

elements.element: Vendor grants Customer a licence covering any Vendor IP embedded in deliverables.
elements.evidence: IBM grants a licence to Type II Materials, but the clause does not universally cover IBM IP embedded in every deliverable. Materials may be designated Type I or otherwise, and the Type I fragment contains no operative licensor-to-licensee grant.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor IP embedded in deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: Only the Type II licence expressly states that it is perpetual; the clause does not provide this duration for Vendor IP embedded in every category of deliverable.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor IP embedded in deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence is irrevocable, but no effective, universal embedded-IP licence covering every deliverable is provided.

elements.element: The licence to Vendor IP embedded in deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: “Paid-up” is a royalty-free equivalent for Type II Materials, but that protection is not established for Vendor IP embedded in every deliverable category.

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: The clause states: “As between the parties, Customer retains all right, title and interest in the Content and all other Customer data.”

elements.element: The clause creates no joint ownership between Customer and Vendor.
elements.evidence: There is no express exclusion of joint ownership and no complete ownership or assignment regime for all deliverables and work product, leaving potential jointly created items unresolved.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic tools.
elements.evidence: IBM ownership is stated for items classified as Type II Materials, but generic tools are not identified or universally reserved to IBM and Materials may instead be classified as Type I or otherwise.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic know-how.
elements.evidence: The clause does not mention or reserve ownership of generic know-how.

elements.element: Customer receives a licence covering every deliverable.
elements.evidence: There is an operative Customer licence only for Type II Materials. Type I Materials are addressed only by an orphaned licence fragment with no identified grantor or grantee, and other classifications may be agreed without stated licence rights.

elements.element: The licence covering every deliverable is perpetual.
elements.evidence: Perpetual duration is stated only for Type II Materials; it is omitted from the Type I fragment and is not guaranteed for other agreed classifications.

elements.element: The licence covering every deliverable is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence is irrevocable, but the clause does not establish an effective irrevocable Customer licence for every deliverable category.

elements.element: The licence covering every deliverable is worldwide.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence is worldwide, but worldwide rights are not operatively secured for every deliverable category.

elements.element: The licence covering every deliverable is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: “Paid-up” is a royalty-free equivalent for Type II Materials, but the clause does not secure that term through an effective Customer licence covering every deliverable.

elements.element: The licence permits Customer to use every deliverable.
elements.evidence: Use rights are expressly granted for Type II Materials, but there is no complete Customer-directed grant covering Type I and other possible deliverable categories.

elements.element: The licence permits Customer to modify every deliverable.
elements.evidence: Modification and derivative-work rights are included for Type II Materials, but are not secured through an effective Customer licence covering every deliverable.

elements.element: The licence permits Customer to sublicense every deliverable.
elements.evidence: Sublicensing is included for Type II Materials, but the clause does not provide an effective sublicensing right for every deliverable category.

elements.element: Customer may exercise the licensed rights for its business.
elements.evidence: The Type II licence allows use for Customer’s business purposes, including through Affiliates and contractors, but that business-purpose right is not secured for every deliverable category.

result.reason: The redline materially improves the Type II licence and expressly protects Customer Data, but it does not give Customer ownership or an assignment of bespoke deliverables and work product. It also does not reach the fallback because the licence protections apply operatively only to Type II Materials, while Type I and other possible classifications remain unresolved, and generic tools and know-how are not expressly reserved. The detached Type I numbered fragment lacks an identified grantor and grantee. The non-operative margin comment cannot cure these omissions.
